# ARC

1. On a grey autumn afternoon at three, chestnuts fall on the cobbles in front of the Nationalmuseum as Fiona, Sarah, Saira, Facundo and Lorena go in wearing the pirate costumes they sewed together out of thin cotton, and Fiona, who sews every seam a second time, wears the wide sash she doubled out of sailcloth and carries her sewing scissors for any loose thread.
2. Because she cannot walk past a crooked old frame in a dusty corner, Fiona straightens it, and a real sea chart slides out from behind it: Kapitän Zollinger's chart, with a red cross on one stone in the old wall under the Lindenhof, above the Limmat.
3. But the guard, Herr Brunner, has seen the chart and strides toward them to lock it in the archive, where nothing found in his museum ever comes out again, so Fiona, who wants to dig out the captain's chest with her own hands, runs with it.
4. So Sarah steps into the narrow passage behind them and chatters questions at Herr Brunner about every suit of armour, and because he will not push a visitor aside, the others reach the back door to the river bank, and then Sarah slips past him and runs after her friends.
5. There, because the chart has left its hiding place, a pirate ship glides out of the fog on the Limmat, and her old steersman calls across that they are Kapitän Zollinger's crew, come for his chart; when Fiona gives her name and the names of her friends, he names the ship the Seeschwalbe and the parrot Pfeffer, who flies line ends through the rigging.
6. Facundo pulls Sarah over the rail one step ahead of Herr Brunner's hand, and the crew, who want their captain's chest raised at last and follow whoever holds his chart, warn that the Seeschwalbe comes only once and sinks back into the fog for good at sunset, so Fiona orders them up the river to the Lindenhof before the sun goes down.
7. But at the low bridge by the Hauptbahnhof the mast must come down, every rope aboard has gone brittle in two hundred years of fog, and when Facundo asks for Fiona's doubled sailcloth sash, the only cloth aboard that will not tear like their thin costumes, she refuses, because she will not spoil her perfect seams.
8. So the rope snaps, and Facundo shouts at everyone to duck and catches the falling mast on his shoulders so nobody is hit, but its tip strikes the bridge, and the yard from which Zollinger once reached his stone breaks off and drifts away.
9. Now the crew must row against the current, and although Saira grabs an oar and calls a fast stroke that brings them to the wall before sunset, Herr Brunner walks the short way through the old town and is on the Lindenhof long before them.
10. The crew hold the Seeschwalbe at the landing with their oars, right under the marked stone, but without the yard the deck lies far below it, the wall is smooth, the sun is sinking behind the hills west of the city, and Herr Brunner, looking down from the Lindenhof, runs for the steps to the landing, where whoever holds the chart can order the crew to pull away.
11. Then Fiona sees an old iron ring above the stone, whose mortar crumbled away long ago, and she cuts her own coat into strips with her sewing scissors and knots them into a rope, because she knows her doubled seams will hold her.
12. She gives the chart to Lorena, whom she trusts most, Pfeffer flies the rope's end through the ring and back down, and Facundo hauls Fiona up the wall, telling her to hold tight above the cold water.
13. Herr Brunner steps aboard and demands the chart, and Lorena wavers for a moment, but then she holds it behind her back and says no, and the crew, who obey whoever holds it, stand between her and him.
14. So Fiona, high on the wall, works the loose stone out with her scissors and her hands, lifts the small chest out of the earth behind it and ties it to her coat-rope, and Facundo lowers first the chest and then Fiona to the deck, the doubled seams holding where the old rope snapped.
15. As the sun goes down, the crew set the five friends, the chest and Herr Brunner ashore on the landing, the Seeschwalbe fades into the fog, and the friends open the chest on a heap of old silver coins; Fiona hands Herr Brunner the chart, which belongs to his museum, and while he stares at the open chest he was too slow to stop, Fiona stands in half a coat and laughs, prouder of it than of any perfect seam.

Challenges taken:
1. The smooth wall with nothing to grip above the deck.
2. A rope built from a sewn coat.
3. Rowing upstream against the current after the mast falls.
4. The chest lowered from a height without breaking.
5. Lorena refuses the chart to someone who keeps demanding it.
